summary: CRA creates a real, dated, per-product obligation and a large pool of EU makers, but the evidence for paid VEX/CSAF triage is developer feature requests, not buyer budgets. The CRA mandates a non-public, top-level SBOM and vulnerability handling, not VEX or CSAF, so many mid-size makers may meet it with free Dependency-Track plus spreadsheets until 2027.

objections.objection: The demand evidence is a handful of developer GitHub issues, not purchase intent from the named buyer. Only one has meaningful engagement (DT #2353, 43 engagement, 13 upvotes over almost four years); the others have 1-7. None comes from a PSIRT lead or regulatory manager at a 50-1,000-person EU maker, and some (rustsec, graal, CycloneDX spec) are open-source maintainers with no budget at all.

The compliance hook is weaker than the pitch implies. The CRA requires an SBOM covering at least top-level dependencies, kept in technical documentation and given to market surveillance authorities on request; it need not be public. VEX/CSAF appear in BSI TR-03183 guidance, not as a CRA obligation. 'Documented vulnerability handling' can be met with free tools plus a log, so VEX publishing is a nice-to-have for most of the target segment unless downstream OEM customers demand it.

Urgency is deadline-shaped and late. The 24h/72h reporting since September 2026 concerns actively exploited vulnerabilities, which a mid-size maker meets rarely and can handle manually; the main obligations land in December 2027. Mid-size firms without a mature PSIRT typically buy compliance tooling close to the deadline or when a customer or authority forces it, so 2027 revenue is likely thin and lumpy for a seed-stage company.

Willingness-to-pay evidence is from enterprise contracts (Interlynk $18k+, Anchore $34.5k+, an undisclosed Manifest medical-device deal), which says nothing about whether mid-size firms already on free Dependency-Track will pay $5.9k for an add-on. The cheapest validated comparable, sbomify at $159/month, already claims a CRA wizard, which anchors this segment's price expectations lower.

The core noise-reduction value (vendor CSAF matching) may be commoditised in the free tool the buyer already runs: DT #2353 is open, but Fraunhofer AISEC reported funding and started work in October 2026, with maintainers asking for an ADR. If it lands within 12-18 months, the 'VEX in a day' wedge shrinks to hosting and publishing.

The size of the market for this exact profile is unquantified: EU makers with 50-1,000 staff that already produce SBOMs and run Dependency-Track and have a named CRA owner. That intersection is probably a few thousand firms at most, and the self-hosting DT users in it skew towards do-it-yourself teams with low willingness to pay.

strongest_point: A binding EU regulation with fixed dates attaches per-product vulnerability-handling duties to tens of thousands of makers, including mid-size firms that enterprise SBOM vendors don't serve.
what_would_change_my_mind: At least 4 of 15 EU CRA owners at 50-500-person makers sign a $490/month pilot LOI (the concept's own test).
At least 8 of 15 show a written VEX/advisory request from a downstream OEM customer or a CRA tooling budget line for 2026-2027.
A draft harmonised standard or market surveillance guidance that expects VEX/CSAF for vulnerability handling.
CSAF matching cuts findings by 50% or more on two real embedded Linux customer SBOMs.
